                                    PROJECT NO. 58000

RULEMAKING TO UPDATE                        §
WHOLESALE AND IOU RETAIL                    §       BEFORE THE PUBLIC UTILITY
TRANSMISSION COST RECOVERY                  §       COMMISSION OF TEXAS
IN THE ERCOT REGION                         §


            COMMENTS OF AFFILIATED ELECTRIC GROUP, LLC (AEG)

                                     I. INTRODUCTION

       AEG, on behalf of our independent school district (ISD) clients and/or colleagues,

including Allen ISD, Cypress Fairbanks ISD, Ennis ISD, Galena Park ISD, Humble ISD, Katy

ISD, Klein ISD, Spring ISD and Spring Branch ISD (collectively referred to as the “Texas Large

ISD’s) respectfully submits these comments regarding the Proposal for Publication in Project No.

58000. AEG appreciates the Commission's efforts to modernize transmission and distribution cost

allocation and supports policies that are equitable, transparent, and administratively practical.

These comments are submitted to ensure that the final rule appropriately considers the unique

operational characteristics of Texas independent school districts (ISDs) and avoids unintended

consequences for Texas students, families, public education, and taxpayers.

       Collectively, the Texas Large ISDs serve more than 425,000 Texas students across

hundreds of campuses and facilities (roughly 1.34% of the entire Texas population pursuant to the

latest U.S. Census estimate of 31,709,821 Texans, and an even higher percentage of Texans in the

ERCOT territory). The chart below breaks down each district’s number of students and facilities,

roughly speaking.

               School District
                                             Students       Schools, Junior Highs and
                                                                 Elementary Schools)

          Cypress-Fairbanks ISD               118,000                              91
          Ennis ISD                             6,626                              12
          Galena Park ISD                      21,366                              26
          Humble ISD                           48,257                              50
          Katy ISD                             96,000                              81

          Spring ISD                           33,575                              41
          Spring Branch ISD                    32,668                              42
          Combined                            429,686                             419


                   II. RESPONSE TO PUCT DRAFT RECOMMENDATIONS

       Because Texas ISDs may be uniquely affected by the proposed methodology, AEG submits

these comments on behalf of the Texas Large ISDs to provide the Commission with practical

information regarding school operations and potential impacts and related proposals.

                                 III. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

•   ISDs operate under fixed public budgets and generally have limited ability to reduce demand

    during certain periods due to state and regulatorily imposed educational mandates in addition

    to student and teacher safety concerns (it’s not merely money or profits on the line, with ISDs’

    operations).

•   A uniform methodology may unintentionally shift additional costs to school districts without

    providing corresponding operational flexibility and to the detriment of districts, students, and

    taxpayers across Texas.




                                                 2
 •   The Commission should assess to what extent tailored treatment, a transition mechanism, or

    another reasonable accommodation for ISDs is most appropriate.

•   The requested consideration is intended to support the Commission's policy objectives while

    avoiding unintended impacts on public schools, Texas families and Texas taxpayers.

                                      IV. BACKGROUND

       Project No. 58000 follows the Commission's earlier consideration of related issues in

Project No. 58484. While significant stakeholder input was provided in the earlier project, Project

No. 58000 provides the opportunity to comment on the specific proposed rule language before

adoption.

                                        V. COMMENTS

A. Texas ISDs Have Unique Operating Characteristics

       Public school districts differ from many commercial and industrial customers. They are

taxpayer-funded public entities, operate on fixed budgets, and strive to maintain safe learning

environments. During certain periods, meaningful load reductions may be impractical without

affecting educational operations, health, safety, or legally required services. Unlike many

commercial customers, ISDs cannot simply shut down or significantly curtail operations to reduce

peak electricity charges while their schools and facilities are in operation without additional

considerations beyond what a commercial enterprise or datacenter is positioned to consider

(nobody wants any student to freeze or overheat). ISDs have far more at stake, versus commercial

customers with mostly only profits and losses to be considered.

B. A Uniform Methodology May Produce Unintended Results

       AEG, on behalf of Large Texas ISDs, encourages the Commission to evaluate whether

applying a single methodology across all customer classes could disproportionately affect ISDs




                                                3
 because, with missions differing from commercial customers seeking solely profits and subject to

legal and regulatory requirements to keep children in school, safe and learning, school districts

generally cannot respond to price signals or peak events in the same manner as many commercial

or industrial customers, nor should they be expected to.

C. The Commission Should Consider Tailored Treatment for ISDs

    Rather than seeking preferential treatment, AEG, on behalf of Large Texas ISDs, respectfully

requests that the Commission implement an approach accommodating the unique characteristics

of ISDs, to justify a tailored implementation approach, transition period, optional election, rational

exceptions, and another reasonable accommodation. Potential considerations before final rule

adoption include:

•   Chiefly, allow ISDs to be billed under the lower of (a) the existing 4CP methodology or (b)

    the new 12CP methodology, which is necessary to ensure ISDs really do benefit from this new

    allocation methodology and system (as further explained below);

•   Consider additional appropriate protections, exemptions, or other mechanisms to ensure that

    any transition to a new Transmission and Distribution Provider (“TDSP”) charge methodology

    does not result in a net increase in charges for ISDs compared with the existing 4CP system;

•   Consider revisions or implementation mechanisms that recognize the operational realities of

    public schools; and

•   Adopt final rule language that avoids unintended adverse impacts on Texas ISDs or any

    increases to their TDSP charges.

D. Many Texas ISDs Have Made Significant Prior Investments in 4CP Management Yet

Districts May Have Differing Equipment and Systems from one Texas ISD to another Texas

ISD.



                                                  4
     The existing 4CP system may be far from perfect, but many ISDs already have systems and

controls designed around it. Many ISDs have already invested substantial resources in

infrastructure, energy management systems, controls, and operational strategies designed to

optimize efficiency and manage TDSP charges under the existing 4CP methodology. For some, a

transition to a new methodology may require additional analysis, planning, and potentially new

investments. At the same time, the existing 4CP system puts ISDs in the same “bucket” as

industrial commercial customers with the same (occasionally punitive) mechanisms designed to

deter electricity usage during peak periods. It is not logical to always treat a large end user of

electricity (with governmental mandates or initiatives to stay in operation and to ensure child

safety) the same as a for profit industrial business who can, if usage or money is on the line on a

hot afternoon, simply shut down and send their employees home, or rather, keep operating as usual

despite the higher costs. With each ISD tending to differ in its own operations and by region,

allowing each ISD an exemption or status pursuant to which it will get the benefits of the new

12CP methodology or the present 4cp methodology (whichever is more cost-effective) could better

allow the new methodology to become implemented without disrupting ISD’s power costs or

operations, to the detriment of Texas families, students and tax payers. Ultimately, Texas residents

and tax payers are the ones who largely foot the bill for the utility charges imposed by the TDSPs

onto the districts.

E. Elevated Energy Costs

    Texas ISDs, as with every other end user of electricity in Texas, already face the prospect of

higher energy costs than in prior years, with the commodity portion of electricity rates having

increased substantially since data centers and hyper-scalers poured into Texas particularly starting

in early 2024 (along with banks/funds purportedly engaging in speculation seeking to profit on the




                                                 5
 AI power trade), and seemingly gobbling up and hoarding much of the state’s wholesale power.

These increased energy charges (for the commodity portion of electricity, i.e., a megawatt hour) is

despite the relatively calm price of natural gas prices during the same period -- as it stands,

wholesale power prices are way higher, yet gas-fired wholesale power is as cheap as (or cheaper

than) ever to produce, with natural gas prices remaining low and historically favorable during peak

summer months. Be that as it may, already faced with higher energy rates for the commodity itself

(the megawatt hours), query whether any new TDSP charge methodology should also be evaluated

in the context of these broader cost pressures facing all Texas end-users, including Texas schools

and taxpayers. Unlike private commercial or industrial customers, increased transmission charges

imposed on school districts are not absorbed by shareholders or discretionary business operations

but instead are passed through to the public (residents and homeowners across Texas) and

ultimately may also reduce funds available for educational purposes. Indeed, Texas families may

otherwise incur a double or triple “whammy” pursuant to the Commission’s present proposal;

unless the aforesaid approach and other measures are carefully implemented, Texas residents could

also face the double whammy of not only higher energy bills for themselves, but also higher state

and local taxes relating to needs to pay local governmental entities’ increased TDSP charges

(unnecessarily). Accordingly, the Commission should consider a separate rate class and a lower

transmission cost allocation magnifier for school districts to ensure they receive a meaningful net

reduction in TDSP charges under any new methodology.

   The Texas ISD’s approach, i.e., allow ISDs to constitute a special rate class to be billed under

the lower of (a) the existing 4CP methodology or (b) the new 12CP methodology, is necessary to

ensure that Texas ISDs obtain the intended benefit from this new methodology in all cases, while




                                                6
 preventing disruption to Texas ISD operations.* If the new 12CP methodology is really supposed

to benefit (and be cheaper) for Texas ISDs, there is no reason not to implement this proposal.

VII. CONCLUSION

       AEG appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments on behalf of the Texas ISDs

and respectfully requests that the Commission consider the recommendations set forth above when

adopting the final rule in Project No. 58000. Please also let us know if any additional information

or summaries would be helpful.

                                             Respectfully submitted,



                                             /s/Rob Potosky
                                             Robert S. Potosky
                                             Chief Legal Officer
                                             Affiliated Electric Group, LLC d/b/a AEG
                                             2401 Fountain View, Ste 462
                                             Houston, Texas 77057
                                             regulatory@affiliatedenergy.com
                                             Phone: 888.728.9885
                                             Bar No. 24027630




*These comments are submitted collectively on behalf of the participating school districts and
participation in these comments does not bind any participating school district to a particular
position in any future proceeding, and each such district reserves the right to take positions
appropriate to its individual circumstances.
